q: Sam saves a new name, the page reloads, and he sees the old name for a moment. Nothing crashed. What happened?
options: The write went to the leader, but the read went to a follower that did not have the copy yet, so it was a stale read
The leader refused the write
The database lost the write
The follower is broken and must be restarted
why: Copies need time to arrive. A follower can return a stale read even when nothing is broken. In the lesson run the follower was wrong for exactly 3 ticks, the copy delay, and then it agreed.

q: What is the usual fix for Sam's stale read, and why does it only need to last a few seconds?
options: Send all reads to the leader for ever, because followers are not reliable
Turn off the followers and keep one copy
For a few seconds after Sam writes, send his reads to the leader. That is longer than the usual copy delay, so after that the follower has the change
Make Sam wait 10 minutes after every write
why: This is read your own writes. Nobody minds if a stranger sees the old name for a moment, but everybody minds when their own change disappears. The cost is a little more work on the leader.

q: Which promise fits each feature: a points balance before a redeem, and a page view counter?
options: Eventual for the balance, strong for the counter
Strong for the balance, eventual for the counter
Strong for both, because strong is safest
Eventual for both, because it is faster
why: A wrong balance means a wrong spend, so it is strong. Nobody checks the last digit of a view counter, so it can be eventual. Choose per feature. Strong costs waiting and sometimes an error.

q: The line between two nodes is cut. Ann bought the last seat on Node A. Ben asks Node B, which still says 1 seat. What does CAP say Node B must do?
options: Nothing, because CAP only matters for slow pages
Both refuse and answer, because you can have all three letters
Pick any 2 of 3 letters for the whole system for ever
Choose: refuse, which is consistent, or answer from its own copy, which is available but may be wrong
why: You cannot drop P, because networks do break. So during a split you choose C or A. Neither choice is free: a refusal gives Ben an error, and an answer can sell the same seat twice.

q: A user in Jakarta reads data whose newest copy is in London, and the strong answer waits for that copy. The network is working fine. Is this a CAP choice?
options: Yes, CAP also covers slow pages
No. There is no split, and you still pay. This is the everyday choice of waiting time against freshness, called PACELC
Yes, but only if the copy is in another country
No. Waiting for the newest copy is free when the network works
why: CAP only speaks when the line is cut. On a normal day, waiting for the newest copy is fresh but slower, and answering at once from a nearby copy is fast but maybe old. A copy in another city adds tens of milliseconds or more.

q: Someone says "one Postgres on one machine is CP." What is the best reply?
options: Correct, all relational databases are CP
No, it is AP because it is always up
One machine has no split, so CAP does not apply to it. The question starts when you add a replica
It is CP only when you turn on strong consistency
why: One label per database hides the real answer. Many stores let you choose for each request or each feature, so say what each feature needs.
